cards.back: The species formed when an acid donates a proton.
A representation of electron delocalization using multiple Lewis contributors with unchanged atomic positions.
A concerted bimolecular nucleophilic substitution with backside attack and inversion at a stereogenic center.
A substituent that departs with the bonding electron pair during a reaction.
A dihedral angle near 180° between bonds that align for concerted elimination.
Preference for forming one constitutional isomer over another.
Addition to a carbonyl followed by elimination of a leaving group at an acyl carbon.
The intermediate formed after nucleophilic addition converts trigonal-planar carbonyl carbon to tetrahedral geometry.
Acyl phosphate ≈ anhydride > thioester > ester > amide > carboxylate.
Poor 3p–2p overlap gives little resonance stabilization, so acetyl-CoA transfers acyl groups readily.
Protonated fraction of a base = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)); only the neutral amine is nucleophilic.
f_ss = k_m/(k_m + k_d): slow turnover lets slow chemistry modify a large fraction.
One step, back-side attack; rate = k[RX][Nu]; methyl > 1° > 2°; strong Nu, polar aprotic solvent; inversion.
Carbocation intermediate; rate = k[RX]; 3° and resonance-stabilized; polar protic solvent; racemization.
Up to 2ⁿ for n stereocenters, fewer with meso forms.
ee = |α_obs/α_pure| × 100; major fraction = (100 + ee)/2.
Valence-electron and unsaturation counts constrain candidates without uniquely identifying one structure.
Keep atoms/sigma connectivity fixed and move paired electrons without exceeding valence.
K=10^(pK_a conjugate acid of base − pK_a donor acid) requires matching conventions.
Proton-transfer favorability and nucleophilic reaction rate are distinct comparisons.
Normalize each state weight and include equivalent-state degeneracy.
Horizontal groups point toward and vertical groups away; reverse apparent traversal when priority four is toward.
R/S does not predict optical-rotation sign; changed product priorities can alter descriptor behavior after spatial inversion.
2ⁿ is an upper bound; actual symmetry can identify configurations such as a meso form.
SN2 forms/leaves bonds together; E2 connects beta proton removal, new π bonding and leaving-pair departure.
Constant effective rates add for substrate disappearance and normalize for branch fractions.
For conventional chair E2, check an axial leaving group and opposite axial beta H in the same conformation.
An empirical time law or substrate category alone does not uniquely establish an elementary mechanism.
Donor pair to carbon and π pair to oxygen preserve carbon valence and require explicit charge accounting.
O pair restores C=O while the C–Z pair leaves with the declared outgoing group.
A net acid/amine condensation equation omits activation, proton and competing-pathway questions.
Fixed free donor and closed total donor are different amount constraints.
Carbon- and oxygen-centered forms represent one delocalized species, not proton-transfer isomers.
Donor alpha carbon joins acceptor carbonyl carbon; acceptor oxygen becomes the alcohol after proton transfer.
The selected addition retains both carbonyl inventories; water loss belongs to a separate transformation.
Possible crossed partners and alpha sites require explicit accounting rather than one desired drawing.
Formula, vibrational and proton patterns constrain different aspects of candidate identity.
n+1 is a selected equivalent-neighbor first-order model, not a universal multiplet rule.
Integral or peak area needs species counts and a justified response model before becoming amount.
Shared achiral spectra do not distinguish enantiomers; retention or optical sign alone does not assign R/S.
Target product equals branch fraction times converted amount in the constant parallel network.
Reaction branching, subsequent recovery and detector reporting are separate operations.
Signed excess uses calibrated A/B amounts; unequal reporting gains bias an area-only ratio.
A proposed activation route and a new signal still need independent structural and material checks.
Blank subtraction corrects an additive offset; separate standard normalization corrects each channel gain.
Convert each reporting channel to amount before calculating pair fractions or excess.
(A−B)/(A+B) distinguishes imbalance from major fraction and retains the declared A/B sign.
Given optical identities do not assign R/S; response calibration does not prove real purity, coelution absence or linearity.
Check cyclic structure, planarity, continuous p-orbital overlap and then a 4n+2 π-electron count.
A planar, continuously conjugated 4n-electron ring is antiaromatic; a system that cannot maintain planarity or continuous overlap is nonaromatic.
π attack forms a nonaromatic σ complex; deprotonation at the substituted carbon restores the aromatic ring.
Halogens deactivate by induction but direct ortho/para through lone-pair resonance donation.
Nucleophile adds to the ipso carbon to form an anionic Meisenheimer complex; the halide then leaves and aromaticity returns.
Electron-withdrawing groups ortho or para to the leaving group delocalize the anion's charge; a meta group cannot by resonance.
With activated rings, addition is usually rate-determining, so aryl fluorides commonly react faster than chlorides, reversing the SN2 order.
For the usual carbocation model, H adds to the less substituted alkene carbon and the other group to the more substituted carbon; this says nothing by itself about syn/anti geometry.
A bridged halonium intermediate is opened from the opposite face, giving anti addition in the standard model.
Hydroboration places B at the less substituted carbon and adds H/B syn; oxidation replaces C–B with C–OH, giving net syn non-Markovnikov hydration.
One HX or X₂ addition consumes the alkene π bond; check atoms and confirm the degree of unsaturation drops by one.
Standard terminal-alkyne hydration forms an enol, then tautomerizes: Markovnikov hydration gives a ketone; hydroboration–oxidation can give an aldehyde.
Move one proton and the π bond to convert enol to carbonyl; the molecular formula is conserved.
One H₂ equivalent removes one of the two π bonds; the standard Lindlar model gives a cis alkene and dissolving-metal reduction gives a trans alkene.
A triple bond takes two H₂ equivalents to reach an alkane; verify the final hydrogen count and zero degrees of unsaturation.

cards.front: Which atoms should remain labelled through an aldol atom map?
cards.back: Label both carbonyl carbons and oxygens and the donor alpha carbon. The new carbon-carbon bond changes connectivity without discarding the donor carbonyl.

cards.front: Why check addition before subtracting water?
cards.back: The beta-hydroxy addition product retains both reactants’ atoms. Subtracting water too early erases the distinction between addition and the later elimination.

cards.front: Why does oxygen not appear in the simple neutral C/H/O unsaturation formula?
cards.back: Divalent oxygen does not change the saturated hydrogen-count relation. The formula count still must be reconciled with a chemically valid connectivity.

cards.front: What is the denominator of an intramolecular proton integral?
cards.back: It counts proton contributions within the stipulated observation model. It is not automatically a mole fraction of separate chemical components or an isolated yield.

cards.front: Why do two stereogenic centers not mean that configurations have been assigned?
cards.back: Counting potential stereogenic elements is a connectivity exercise. Assigning configurations requires additional stereochemical information and a justified observation model.

cards.front: Does product renumbering physically move a carbon tag?
cards.back: No. Preserve the original atom map first; a change of naming origin is distinct from skeletal rearrangement.

cards.front: Why include a separate protonation after nucleophile addition?
cards.back: Addition leaves an anionic carbon at the other aryne endpoint; its protonation completes the stated product and hydrogen ledger.

cards.front: Which denominator does a branch selectivity use?
cards.back: It describes allocation among the specified consumed/product channels, which differs from yield relative to initial starting inventory.

cards.front: Does consistency with a mechanism prove it uniquely?
cards.back: No. Name the alternative mechanisms, observations, assignment controls and limitations that the evidence actually addresses.

cards.front: What must follow a retrosynthetic disconnection?
cards.back: A forward audit of bond formation, functional-group compatibility, stereochemistry, atom conservation and evidence for selectivity.

cards.front: Are percentages from different stages additive?
cards.back: No. Step losses act on successive inventories; use defined fractional yields and keep conversion, isolation and purity separate.

cards.front: Does one new stereogenic center imply an assigned enantiomer?
cards.back: No. Absolute configuration and enantiomeric composition need suitable evidence; an achiral paper route supplies no automatic enantioselectivity.

cards.front: Can protection be treated as a free planning symbol?
cards.back: No. Its formation, survival and removal add compatibility/evidence requirements and can add losses, even when a paper matrix stipulates them.

cards.front: Which independent checks should an aryl evidence report include?
cards.back: Preserve original atom labels, test mechanism-predicted attachments, close the amount ledger and distinguish observed quantities from stipulated branching.

cards.front: Why keep the tag map when product names change?
cards.back: A product may be renumbered for naming; the original tagged carbon still identifies the physical atom and its relationship to the new bond.

cards.front: What distinguishes the methyl and ethyl route examples stereochemically?
cards.back: Methyl addition creates two identical methyl substituents at the alcohol carbon; ethyl addition gives methyl and ethyl as different substituents.

cards.front: What should a complete route report separate?
cards.back: Structure/atom bookkeeping, mechanistic compatibility, stereochemistry, synthetic-yield definitions and evidence that the proposed operations actually perform selectively.
